implementation_notes: Cuckoo generates mock subclasses from classes and protocols at build time; a generated spy is a mock whose calls are forwarded to the victim by default (MockGreeter().withEnabledSuperclassSpy()), and stubbing/verification use stub(mock) { ... when(...) } and verify(mock.method()).wasCalled(). What replaces the classic hand-written spy is the generated subclass plus the forwarding flag - third-party code generation, so build setup is part of the cost.
code_sketch:
let spy = MockGreeter().withEnabledSuperclassSpy()   // forwards to the victim
greeterService.greet(using: spy)                     // real method runs
verify(spy.greetWithMessage("Hello")).wasCalled()
pitfalls: Cuckoo needs a build phase that regenerates mocks whenever protocols or classes change; stale generated files fail the build or silently miss members.
withEnabledSuperclassSpy forwards to the victim, but any stubbed member stops running the real implementation - over-stubbing turns the spy back into a stub.

variants.name: Hand-written protocol-conforming spy
variants.idiom_name: final class SpyMailer: Mailer with a recorded call log
variants.implementation_notes: Without generated tooling, the Swift spy is a class conforming to the collaborator protocol that forwards to a wrapped instance (or records only) and exposes its log to the test; protocols are the seam XCTest relies on, and because a protocol defines the requirements conforming types must implement, the spy cannot silently drift from the interface. What replaces the classic spy object is this hand-written conformer - more code, but no build-phase codegen and no third-party dependency.
pitfalls: Sharing one spy instance across tests leaks recorded calls; create it per test and keep the log private(set).
Protocols with associated types or generic requirements cannot be stored as plain existentials, so the seam may need type erasure or generics to accept the spy.
